narration: Here is the whole solution on one slide. A user program calls m protect. A tiny assembly stub raises a software interrupt. The kernel dispatches to sys m protect, which fetches the two arguments and calls one shared helper, set u v m write. The helper validates the whole range first, then clears or sets only the writable bit, then reloads C R 3 to flush the T L B. The same helper serves m unprotect, so the two calls cannot drift apart. We then close a second door: system calls that write into user buffers must check the destination is writable, or the kernel itself would fault.

`sys_mprotect` fetches `addr` and `len`
`setuvmwrite()` validates the whole range first
Then it changes only `PTE_W` and reloads `CR3`
`read`, `fstat`, `pipe` now check their output buffers

narration: We copied the pattern of an existing call, uptime. In usys dot S, the S Y S C A L L macro defines a function that loads the system call number into E A X, executes int T underscore S Y S C A L L, and returns. Our two additions are the last two lines: S Y S C A L L m protect and S Y S C A L L m unprotect. The prototypes in user dot h let user programs compile against them. Nothing else is needed on the user side.

narration: On the kernel side, syscall dot h gives each call a unique number: twenty-two for m protect and twenty-three for m unprotect. In syscall dot c, we declare the two handlers with extern, and add two entries to the dispatch table, indexed by those numbers. When the trap arrives, the function syscall reads the number from E A X, looks it up in the table, calls the handler, and stores the return value back in E A X. That return value is what the user program sees as the result of m protect.

narration: In sysproc dot c, change protection is the common front end. It fetches the first and second arguments with arg int. Remember arg int reads the word at stack pointer plus four plus four times n, skipping the return address. It then calls set u v m write with the current process's page directory, its size, the address, the length, and a flag: one for writable, zero for read-only. sys m protect passes zero. sys m unprotect passes one. One helper, two thin wrappers. Notice what is not here: no validation. The helper does all the checking, so the rules live in exactly one place.

narration: Now the heart of the project, set u v m write in vm dot c. It receives the page directory, the process size sz, the start address, the page count, and the desired state. The first check rejects an unaligned address, a count of zero or less, and a start at or beyond the process size. Because the count is a signed integer, negatives are caught here too. The second check is subtle. We do not compute address plus count times 4096 yet, because that product can overflow thirty-two bits. Instead we compare the count with how many whole pages fit between the start and the end of the process. Only after that is the end address safe to compute. Then pass one: for every page, walk the page table without allocating, and require the entry to exist, be present, and be a user page. The stack guard page has its user bit cleared, so it fails here.

narration: Pass two runs only after pass one succeeded for every page, so it cannot fail halfway. That is how a bad page in the middle of a range never leaves a partial change. For each page we either OR in the writable bit, or AND with its inverse. All other bits, including the physical address, are untouched. Finally, lcr3 of V two P of the page directory reloads C R 3 and flushes this processor's T L B. We need V two P because C R 3 takes a physical address while the page directory pointer is a kernel virtual address. Without this line, the processor could keep using a cached writable translation, and the next write would wrongly succeed.

commentHints.comment: pass 1 loop ends: every page is valid
pass 2: only now do we modify anything

reloading `CR3` flushes it; `V2P` makes the address physical

narration: Let us make the overflow concrete. Suppose the start address is 0x1000 and the count is 0x100000, which is two to the twentieth. Multiply the count by 4096, which is two to the twelfth, and you get two to the thirty-second. In thirty-two bit arithmetic that wraps around to zero. A naive check that computes start plus count times 4096 would see an end of 0x1000, which looks perfectly valid. Our check compares the count with the number of pages that actually fit, and correctly rejects it. If your professor asks why we wrote the check that way, this is the answer.

bullets: start = `0x1000`, count = `0x100000` (2^20 pages)
`count * 4096` is 2^32, which wraps to 0 in 32 bits
Naive end address = `0x1000`: looks valid, but is wrong
Ours: `count > (sz - va) / PGSIZE` is rejected correctly
Also catches negative counts and addresses that wrap

narration: Two design decisions deserve a clear answer. Why two passes? The specification says a failed call must leave previous permissions unchanged. If we changed pages while validating, a bad page late in the range would leave the earlier pages already modified. Validating everything first makes the update pass unable to fail. Why the T L B flush? Our own test proves it matters. A child first writes a page, so the processor caches a writable translation. It then calls m protect and writes again with no context switch. Only the C R 3 reload makes that second write fault. Earlier tests missed this, because a freshly forked child reloads C R 3 anyway. So we added a dedicated test.

bullets: Two passes make a failed call change nothing
Merging them left a program page read-only after a rejected range
`lcr3` flushes cached permissions so protection is immediate
A dedicated test fails if the flush is removed
Fork hid the bug in the first version of the tests

narration: Fork needed no change. Look at the existing copy u v m. For every page of the parent, it reads the flags with P T E underscore F L A G S, allocates a fresh physical page, copies the contents, and maps the child's copy with the same flags. So if the parent page is read-only, the child's copy is read-only too. That is inheritance. The two copies are different physical pages with different P T Es. Later changes by one process cannot affect the other. Our tests check both directions: a child unprotecting its copy leaves the parent protected, and a child protecting its copy leaves the parent writable.

narration: Now the problem we found by testing. A user write to a protected page faults in user mode, and the process dies. But what if the kernel writes into a protected user page for the user? The read system call copies data into a user buffer from inside the kernel. Because C R 0 W P is set, a kernel write to a read-only page faults in kernel mode. The trap handler treats any kernel fault as a kernel bug and calls panic. We reproduced this: read from a pipe into a protected page crashed the guest with panic trap, before the fix. The rule we adopted: if the kernel will write into a user buffer, check that every page of it is writable first, and return minus one if not. If the kernel only reads the buffer, as write does, a protected page is fine.

bullets: `read()` into a protected page: kernel-mode write fault
`trap()` treats kernel-mode faults as bugs: `panic: trap`
Fix: check output buffers are writable, return `-1` if not
`write()` only READS the buffer, so protected sources are fine
`copyout()` also honours `PTE_W`

narration: The new function check u v m write takes a page directory, a start address, and a length. A length of zero is fine, nothing will be written. Otherwise it computes the last byte's page, and loops from the first page to the last, so buffers that span several pages are covered, including a writable page followed by a protected one. For each page, all three bits must be set: present, user, and writable. The expression masks the entry with the three flags and compares with all three. Anything less returns minus one. Like pass one of our main helper, it never allocates, so checking cannot change the page tables.

narration: In syscall dot c, the existing arg ptr only checks that the buffer lies inside the process. Our arg ptr w builds on it. It calls arg ptr first. If that fails, return minus one. Otherwise it calls check u v m write for the same range, so the buffer must also be writable. Using one new function keeps the three callers identical. The size argument is the buffer length that the system call will write.

narration: Three system calls write into user memory, and each changed by exactly one word: arg ptr became arg ptr w. In sys read, the destination buffer p is checked before file read copies data into it. In sys fstat, the struct stat that will be filled is checked. In sys pipe, the two-integer array that receives the file descriptors is checked. Notice what did not change: sys write still uses plain arg ptr, because it only reads the user buffer. Our test confirms that writing from a protected page prints the data.

narration: One more door. Copy out writes through the kernel's own mapping of the physical page, which is always writable. It would silently bypass a read-only user mapping. So after finding the kernel address, we also call check u v m write for that one page, and fail if it is not writable. In today's x v 6 the only caller is exec, which writes to a brand-new stack, so behaviour does not change. But the protection guarantee is now complete.
